articles.title: Advanced Iterative Metal Artifact Reduction With Intrinsic Spectral Information From Photon-counting Detector Computed Tomography: Improving the Assessment of Metal-bone Interface.
articles.authorString: Demmert TT, Schikorra T, Heining SM, Specovius A, Klambauer K, Moser LJ, Mergen V, Schmidt B, Flohr T, Eberhard M, Alkadhi H.
articles.abstractText:
Background

Metallic implants can cause relevant artifacts in computed tomography (CT) imaging, affecting the quality and diagnostic utility of scans. Previous advancements in metal artifact reduction techniques have shown promise but still exhibit limitations in artifact reduction, particularly close to metal implants.

Purpose

To evaluate a novel, advanced iterative metal artifact reduction (iMAR) algorithm for photon-counting detector CT in an experimental study focused on visualizing the vicinity of a fixation nail implant.

Methods

Three bovine femur bones with titanium-based trochanteric fixation nail implants were scanned on a clinical photon-counting detector CT scanner. Images were reconstructed (1) without iMAR, (2) with the current iMAR algorithm, and (3) with a new prototype iMAR algorithm. The new iMAR prototype algorithm advances state-of-the-art iMAR for photon-counting detector CT by utilizing intrinsically available spectral information. Attenuation and artifact severity (SD of attenuation) were quantified by placing regions-of-interest on each reconstruction across 3 different axial slices: One in the bone marrow immediately adjacent to the metal implant and one in the water adjacent to the femur with the implant. Qualitative image quality, newly introduced artifacts, and diagnostic confidence were rated by 3 radiologists using 5-point Likert scales. Differences between reconstructions were tested using the Friedman test with Wilcoxon post hoc tests; interreader agreement was assessed using Krippendorff alpha.

Results

Artifact severity in the bone adjacent to the implant significantly decreased from 226 HU (no iMAR) to 174 HU (current iMAR) and to 159 HU with the new iMAR ( P < 0.001). Adjacent to the femur, artifact severity decreased from 63 HU to 48 HU and to 29 HU, respectively ( P < 0.05). Qualitative scores differed significantly between reconstructions ( P < 0.05), with highest ratings for new iMAR across all categories. Current iMAR introduced new artifacts near the implant, which did not occur with new iMAR ( P < 0.05).

Conclusion

Experimental evidence from a bovine femur implant model suggests that a new, advanced iterative metal artifact reduction algorithm leveraging intrinsic spectral information from photon-counting detector CT effectively reduces metal artifacts and further improves the visualization of the metal-bone interface. Thus, this technique has the potential to enhance the assessment of implant-related complications such as aseptic loosening.

articles.abstractText:
Background

The facial artery is the principal arterial supply to the midface and is among the most frequently encountered vascular structures during facial reconstructive, aesthetic, and minimally invasive procedures. Precise knowledge of its anatomical course and morphometric characteristics is essential to minimize vascular complications. However, previous morphometric studies have largely been descriptive and have rarely accounted for bilateral anatomical correlation or simultaneously evaluated the independent effects of age, sex, and laterality using appropriate multivariable statistical models.

Methods

A retrospective cross-sectional study was performed using computed tomography angiography (CTA) examinations from 103 adults, yielding 201 evaluable facial arteries. Standardized three-dimensional morphometric measurements were obtained at the inferior border of the mandible and the lateral alar base. Linear mixed-effects models incorporating patient-specific random intercepts were used to evaluate the effects of age, sex, side, and CTA diagnostic category while accounting for within-subject correlation. Measurement reproducibility was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman analysis, and Cohen's kappa.

Results

Type III, according to the Furukawa classification, was the predominant anatomical pattern (67.2%). Among 98 patients with bilateral visualization, Furukawa type showed complete right-left concordance (100%; κ = 1.00). In an additional patient-level logistic model, neither age (OR 0.992 per year; 95% CI, 0.965-1.020; P = 0.584) nor female sex (OR 1.793; 95% CI, 0.767-4.191; P = 0.178) was significantly associated with Type III versus Type II. For continuous morphometric variables, no systematic laterality effect was detected, although individual-level bilateral agreement varied across parameters. After Holm correction across morphometric outcomes, women had a smaller facial artery diameter at the inferior border of the mandible and a shorter zygomatic arch-facial artery distance than men, while increasing age was independently associated with a shorter oral commissure-facial artery distance. Quantitative morphometric measurements demonstrated good-to-excellent observer reproducibility (intraobserver ICC: 0.900-0.960; interobserver ICC: 0.760-0.860), whereas categorical assessment of facial artery position relative to the nasolabial sulcus showed perfect intraobserver (κ = 1.00) and substantial interobserver agreement (κ = 0.79).

Conclusions

CTA provides a reproducible morphometric assessment of the facial artery. No systematic laterality effect was identified for continuous morphometric variables, although individual bilateral agreement varied by measurement, while Furukawa type showed complete bilateral concordance in patients with both arteries visualized. Age and sex were not significantly associated with Furukawa Type III versus Type II, but they influenced selected continuous morphometric parameters. These findings characterize facial artery anatomy in a Mexican clinical cohort and may inform individualized anatomical assessment and preprocedural planning; they do not establish procedural risk thresholds.

articles.abstractText:
Background

Optimal mucosal visualization is essential for high-quality esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), particularly for the detection of subtle upper gastrointestinal lesions. Oral simethicone and N-acetylcysteine (NAC) are commonly used to improve mucosal cleanliness, whereas lidocaine ice popsicles provide effective topical pharyngeal anesthesia for unsedated EGD. We evaluated whether incorporating simethicone and NAC into a lidocaine ice popsicle could improve mucosal visibility while maintaining patient comfort.

Methods

This single-center, prospective, double-blind, randomized controlled trial enrolled 374 adults undergoing unsedated diagnostic EGD between December 2024 and June 2025. Participants were randomized (1:1) to receive either a lidocaine ice popsicle containing simethicone (100 mg) and NAC (600 mg) or a conventional lidocaine ice popsicle. The primary outcome was mucosal visibility assessed using a modified Total Visibility Score (TVS). Secondary outcomes included procedure time, water volume required for mucosal cleansing, additional simethicone use, endoscopist satisfaction, ease of esophageal instrumentation, gag reflex, patient satisfaction, discomfort, pain, and adverse events. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

Results

All 374 randomized participants (187 per group) completed the study and were analyzed according to their assigned groups. Baseline characteristics were descriptively similar between groups. The intervention group had a significantly lower TVS than the control group (6.19 ± 0.51 vs. 10.39 ± 2.22; mean difference, -4.20; 95% CI, -4.53 to -3.88; P < 0.001), indicating better mucosal visibility. Exploratory segment-specific analyses showed lower visibility scores in all six gastrointestinal segments. The intervention group also had higher endoscopist satisfaction, shorter procedure time (10.87 ± 1.44 vs. 12.75 ± 0.96 min; P < 0.001), lower water requirements for mucosal cleansing, and less frequent use of additional diluted simethicone during EGD (12.8% vs. 96.8%; P < 0.001). Exploratory analyses showed statistically significant differences in gag reflex and pain scores, although the absolute differences were small. Patient satisfaction, discomfort, and ease of esophageal instrumentation did not differ significantly between groups. No adverse events were observed during the defined observation period.

Conclusions

The combined formulation of simethicone and N-acetylcysteine incorporated into a lidocaine ice popsicle improved mucosal visibility compared with a lidocaine ice popsicle alone during unsedated EGD and was associated with improved procedural efficiency. This integrated formulation may provide a practical approach to pre-endoscopic preparation by combining topical anesthesia with mucosal cleansing. Further multicenter studies are warranted to confirm its effectiveness, generalizability, and safety with longer follow-up.
